source_document.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman speak as they arrive during the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Leaders’ Summit at The Ritz-Carlton on May 14, 2025 in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)
Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has built his rule on security and prosperity, the simple concept that a modernized Saudi Arabia would also be a safer and more prosperous one. However, that promise is now under unprecedented strain.
Repeated missile and drone attacks have targeted Saudi airfields, threatened the Kingdom’s oil-processing hub at Abqaiq and forced the shutdown of the East-West pipeline — the strategic lifeline intended to bypass Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The latest attacks on Riyadh’s international airport have brought the war to the Kingdom’s capital, further exposing the limits of its defenses and the vulnerability of its economic ambitions.
The Prince still retains firm control over the security establishment, faces no organized domestic opposition capable of challenging his rule and commands substantial financial resources. But his unprecedented concentration of power has made him the indispensable center of the Saudi system, while also making the system’s fortunes increasingly inseparable from his own.
It is against this backdrop that Washington is moving forward with a nuclear cooperation agreement that could allow uranium enrichment on Saudi soil. The debate has focused on safeguards, proliferation risks and what the United States might receive in return.
But the Kingdom’s mounting security crisis raises a more fundamental question: What happens when Washington transfers nuclear capabilities designed to last half a century to a political system whose future cannot be confidently predicted? And what can the US Congress do to ensure there are safeguards in place should Saudi policy, by choice or not, change in the coming years?
The agreement signed in July 2026 opens a pathway to enriching uranium on Saudi soil. It provides for a two-year study of commercial enrichment, initially limited to uranium enriched to 5 percent, with additional review before any move toward 20 percent. Under the proposed arrangement, a facility would reportedly be operated by American companies using a “black box” model intended to prevent Saudi personnel from accessing sensitive centrifuge technology. However, the agreement does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Additional Protocol, which provides more intrusive off-site verification measures.
The central problem, however, is not simply whether the proposed safeguards are sufficient. It is the assumption that the political circumstances under which nuclear capabilities are transferred will remain sufficiently stable over the decades in which those capabilities exist.
The current war demonstrates why such an assumption is risky. Despite enormous investments in military modernization, Saudi Arabia has struggled to protect vital infrastructure against comparatively inexpensive missiles and drones. Its efforts to diversify export routes have also revealed their limitations. The East-West pipeline, designed to reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz, became a target itself. Meanwhile, Houthi advances along the Red Sea have threatened another critical maritime passage, Bab el-Mandeb.
The consequences extend beyond immediate military damage. Saudi Arabia’s economic transformation depends on attracting foreign investment, expanding tourism, developing new industries and convincing international businesses that the Kingdom is a safe and predictable environment. Repeated attacks on airports, energy facilities and transportation networks undermine precisely that perception.
External military pressure, damage to critical infrastructure, mounting war costs and declining economic confidence could become far more destabilizing if compounded by a future succession crisis or fractures within the ruling elite or security establishment. Concentration of power can strengthen a regime while its center remains secure, but it can also increase vulnerability if that center comes under strain.
None of this means regime change is imminent; that is the wrong standard for nuclear policy even if it were. Washington does not need to predict the fall of the House of Saud. It needs to recognize that no one can confidently predict the character of the Saudi political order over the lifetime of a nuclear energy program.
The problem becomes considerably more serious when uranium enrichment is involved. Enrichment is not simply another component of civilian nuclear energy. It is a strategic capability that can provide a foundation for a future weapons program. A black-box arrangement may restrict access to centrifuge designs, but it cannot entirely prevent the accumulation of expertise, trained personnel and institutional knowledge. Once these capabilities exist, they cannot simply be recalled if relations with Washington deteriorate or Saudi Arabia’s political order changes.
Saudi leaders have also been unusually explicit about the strategic significance of nuclear capabilities. In 2018, Mohammed bin Salman declared that if Iran developed a nuclear weapon, Saudi Arabia would follow suit. More recently, the Kingdom’s defense agreement with nuclear-armed Pakistan introduced an additional nuclear dimension into Riyadh’s security relationships, even if subsequent Pakistani statements qualified the extent of those commitments.
Iran provides an uncomfortable historical warning. The US helped establish Iran’s civilian nuclear program when the Shah was one of Washington’s closest regional partners. Under Atoms for Peace, Washington supplied Iran’s first research reactor and helped train Iranian nuclear scientists.
Then the political system changed.
The Islamic Republic’s present enrichment capabilities were not simply inherited from the American-supported program, of course. But the larger lesson remains: nuclear institutions, expertise and ambitions can survive the political order under which they were created. Technology can outlive the strategic assumptions that justified its transfer.
Congress should therefore examine more than proliferation safeguards. It should also conduct a political durability assessment. Who would control enrichment capabilities during a future succession crisis? Could nuclear facilities be secured during prolonged regional conflict? What happens if relations with Washington deteriorate? And what political forces might ultimately inherit the infrastructure and expertise the US helped establish?
This does not mean Saudi Arabia should be denied civilian nuclear energy because its political future is uncertain. It means that the more sensitive and enduring the technology being transferred, the less policymakers should rely on confidence in today’s leadership as a substitute for durable safeguards and long-term strategic planning.
Mohammed bin Salman may successfully navigate the present crisis. But nuclear policy must account for the possibility that the Kingdom’s political character will change substantially over time.
The US is considering a decision whose consequences could endure well beyond Mohammed bin Salman and perhaps beyond the present Saudi political order itself. Nuclear reactors can operate for 50 years or more. The infrastructure, expertise and sensitive fuel-cycle capabilities associated with them can outlive governments and even political systems. An agreement concluded with Mohammed bin Salman today could therefore shape the capabilities available to Saudi leaders in the 2050s, 2060s and beyond.
The relevant question is not simply whether Washington trusts Saudi Arabia with sensitive nuclear technology today. It is whether Washington is prepared to trust the Saudi Arabia that might inherit it tomorrow.
Yoel Guzansky heads the Institute for National Security Studies’ Gulf Studies program, served on Israel’s National Security Council (2005-2010), and co-authored Fraternal Enemies: Israel and the Gulf Monarchies (2020).
Henry Sokolski runs the Nonproliferation Policy Education Center in Arlington, Virginia, served as the Pentagon’s deputy for nonproliferation policy (1989-1993) and authored Underestimated: Our Not So Peaceful Nuclear Future (2019).
